item.title: Democrats take control of Congress and put Trump's economic agenda in their sights
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats retook power in Washington on Tuesday, flipping key House and Senate seats to command majorities in both chambers of Congress. The power shift creates a new platform for Democrats to launch investigations of President Trump's economic allies — Elon Musk, to name one — and pass bills that may be unlikely to become law but will mark a sharp change in the political climate for business leaders and economic issues after two years of unified Republican control. The change also appears set to elevate figures like Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren and others to prominent positions with oversight over economic policy. Read more: What a Democratic sweep means for stocks Voter casts their ballot at a polling place on November 3 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images) Jim Vondruska via Getty Images Democrats are planning "a shock-and-awe legislative sprint," the New York Times reported , on issues like healthcare subsidies and Trump's tariffs, which could prompt a wave of bills to pass the House but stall against the 60-vote threshold in the Senate. Even in the minority, Senate rules mean Republicans retain the power to stop legislation. Democrats are also likely to seek areas of bipartisan agreement on pharmaceuticals, the housing market, and AI data centers, all sectors that both Republicans and Democrats have spotlighted on the campaign trail. Divided government, of course, may also set the stage for political clashes that could destabilize markets and the broader economy. "While conventional wisdom suggests equities tend to rally following midterm elections, particularly when the outcome produces divided government, we caution that the post-election environment may look considerably different this cycle," Raymond James Washington Policy Analyst Ed Mills warned in a pre-election note. He added that much of the recent volatility has been driven by unexpected moves from the White House. "We believe Trump will increasingly test the limits of executive authority during the remainder of his term," Mills wrote. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York talks with phone bank volunteers during a midterm election night watch party in Washington on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images) Tom Williams via Getty Images 'Lawyer up': An expected focus on Elon Musk and Trump's economic team The House is set to be led by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who has been notably tight-lipped about his plans . He met with Democratic volunteers as Election Day wound down and told reporters , "We're relentlessly focused on driving down the high cost of living and fighting for an affordable America." Jeffries avoided the question of whether he would reach out to Trump, while the president told the New York Times he will accept the election results . Going by early signals, Democrats intend to aim their new powers at an array of high-profile targets, with Musk chief among them, as part of a far-reaching effort to impose new checks on the Trump administration. "Lawyer up," said Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to become chair of the House Oversight Committee, in one particularly pithy signal of the Democrats' plans. Recent developments involving Elon Musk and Starlink in Ukraine are just the latest topic that Democrats say they will investigate around the world's richest man. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Musk ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine and discussed the decision on a call with Trump in October. A group of Silicon Valley lawmakers said in a letter the issue raises broader concerns and could lead them to "closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk's businesses" in the next Congress. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk receives the National Medal of Science from President Donald Trump during Summit in Washington, DC in October. (Win McNamee/Getty Images) Win McNamee via Getty Images Musk could also face questions about his role in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and SpaceX's other government contracts. Trump this week said he would consider preemptively pardoning officials like Musk who face legal scrutiny from Democrats, saying in an interview , "I would if I needed to, sure. I wouldn't even think about it." Capitol Hill observers are also expecting economic-themed clashes, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent potentially facing new scrutiny. Politico recently reported that Democrats are planning to investigate the Treasury Department and the IRS, as well as Trump's actions to rein in the power of financial regulatory agencies. Bessent's clashes with Democratic lawmakers have already been caustic and highly personal over the last two years, and that could only intensify as Democrats gain the power to subpoena documents and compel testimony, with Sen. Warren likely to lead the Senate's influential Banking Committee. This new subpoena power could also put an array of executives in the hot seat, from tech executives facing potential hearings over harmful AI-agent behavior to CEOs being called to answer allegations of price gouging across sectors. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent testifies during a House Financial Services Committee hearing in September. (ROBERTO SCHMIDT / AFP via Getty Images) ROBERTO SCHMIDT via Getty Images Sectors where 'investors might see a glimmer of hope' The changeover in power has implications — good and bad — for numerous business sectors. Democrats could seek to boost sectors like clean energy by blocking further efforts by Trump to cut tax credits. Stifel Chief Washington Policy Strategist Brian Gardner offered clean energy as the top potential winner in his final midterm election preview. "Investors might see a glimmer of hope that clean energy tax credits could be revived or extended," he wrote this week, adding that the credits "also have some GOP support so they could be revived even in a split Congress." "I will fight to reverse his costly tariffs and devastating health care cuts, and bring an end to the war in Iran," Congressman Brendan Boyle added in a statement Tuesday. Boyle is set to be the next Chairman of the House Budget Committee. Moves to reverse Trump's tariffs are almost sure to be met with a presidential veto, but more bipartisan areas could sidestep the president. Screengrab of a campaign ad from Mike Rogers. The housing issue earlier this year delivered a potential proof of concept when a major piece of legislation passed with bipartisan majorities and became law despite Trump's refusal to sign it . During the now-concluded campaign season, candidates from both parties focused criticisms on pharmaceuticals and AI data centers, a sign that these sectors may be ripe for bipartisan compromise. This story has been updated. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. item.title: Iran says midterms election results show Americans reject the war
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
What to know about the Iran war today: Iran's chief negotiator said Wednesday that the U.S. midterm election results reflected Americans' rejection of the war President Trump launched against his country. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf added a warning that if Mr. Trump does not heed the message from American voters, it will bring "a Nightmare."President Trump acknowledged Tuesday night that the war with Iran was partially to blame for the GOP's resounding midterm elections losses. But Mr. Trump told The Wall Street Journal he didn't regret the conflict and added he "would have done it again."Despite signs of a diplomatic push to reach a peace deal, ships continue to come under attack in the Strait of Hormuz. Four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines while transiting the waterway, Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Wednesday. Houthis claim to have struck Saudi Arabian capital's King Khalid airport again with ballistic missile Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen claimed Wednesday to have struck King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh with a ballistic missile, causing "extensive damage." Saudi Arabia, despite its significant size, wealth and military advantage over the Iran-backed Yemeni rebels, has been unable to stop missile and drone attacks by the group. Previous Houthi strikes on Saudi airports in October killed at least 20 people, most of them at King Khalid. In a statement shared Wednesday on social media, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that the the Riyadh airport was "unsafe" and he renewed the group's "call to all international airlines, employees, and travelers not to travel through Saudi airspace, as it is unsafe, with the exception of the airspace over the holy areas of Mecca and Medina." There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the Houthi claim to have hit the airport again on Wednesday. Houthis claim series of successful attacks on Saudi Arabian forces The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen claimed Wednesday to have shot down a Chinese-made armed reconnaissance drone operated by Saudi Arabia over Yemen's southern Taiz province. In a statement shared online by Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said it was the 10th Saudi operated drone of the type downed by the rebels during the current escalation of Yemen's civil war, in which Saudi Arabia backs the Yemeni government. Saree said in a string of social media posts that the Houthis had also "carried out an operation targeting Saudi enemy forces" with six ballistic missiles east of Yemen's al-Jawf province, "leaving dozens dead and wounded and destroying a number of military vehicles." Other Houthi operations targeted a radar installation north of Jizan, Saudi Arabia, and a Saudi military encampment in Najran, he said. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the Houthi claims. Iranians take to streets of Tehran for pro-regime rally People marched through central Tehran Wednesday in a major pro-regime rally to mark the 47th anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the U.S. embassy in the Iranian capital, chanting anti-U.S. and Israel slogans. Some held signs calling for revenge for the killing of former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the outset of the ongoing war, while others mocked President Trump. "We are not happy about the surge in oil prices," said one woman, who gave AFP only her last name, Mahmoudkhani. "But there is some satisfaction in knowing we are no longer living this torment alone. We, alone, have been suffering under sanctions for so many years," she added. Some echoed Iranian officials doubts' that the election results would change much for Iranians. "Whether it is the Democrats or the Republicans, there is no difference for us," Mohammad, a 42-year-old civil servant, told AFP. "The US government's approach toward the Iranian people has unfortunately remained the same over the past 50 years." CBS/AFP Statement attributed to Iran's supreme leader plays down hopes of shift in U.S. war policy A statement attributed to Iran's elusive Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Wednesday said anyone expecting a shift in U.S. policy regarding the war with Iran in the wake of the American midterm elections was "seriously mistaken." "Those who still harbor even the slightest hope that the behavior of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken," said the statement published on Khamenei's website. Khamenei was named as the successor to his father, former leader Ali Khamenei, soon after the older man was killed in the initial wave of U.S.-Israeli strikes at the outset of the war. U.S. officials believe the younger Khamenei was seriously wounded in the same strike, and he has not been seen or heard from directly at all since being named the new supreme leader. President Trump has said the war with Iran was partly responsible for the dismal midterm election results for his Republican party this week, but that he does not regret his decision to launch it in conjunction with Israel. In the message released Wednesday, Khamenei warned that "should such aggressions be repeated, the war's scope will become much wider." CBS/AFP Trump says U.S. has no immediate plan to strike Iran, despite being "locked and loaded" President Trump told the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday evening that he had no immediate plans to order new strikes on Iran, after keeping the option on the table for weeks ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. "We seem to be getting everything we want," the FT quoted Mr. Trump as saying, referring to the current stalemate with Iran. While major fighting stopped weeks ago, the standoff has seen the Islamic Republic continue threatening and attacking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, which in turn has kept global oil prices 60% to 70% higher than they were before the war started, driving up consumer costs across the globe. Asked whether there would be a new attack on Iran later this week, Mr. Trump said "we're locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it." Despite the impasse, the president claimed the current circumstances were "brilliant," with oil still reaching global markets from the Persian Gulf, including under U.S. military escort through the Strait of Hormuz. "If you think about it, we haven't really had a war with them in a long time. Six months, maybe more," asserted Mr. Trump. China says avoiding more conflict in Middle East a "top priority" China's foreign ministry said Wednesday that avoiding a resumption of the conflict between Iran and the U.S. was a "top priority" in its diplomatic efforts in the region. "The top priority is to avoid the resumption of hostilities in the Middle East that would bring disaster to the region's people," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing. China will "support Iran and the U.S. in resolving disputes through negotiations, promote finding a political settlement to the Yemen issue, to help reach a proper and comprehensive solution for the opening of the Strait of Hormuz," she added. China is an economic ally of Iran. Chinese purchases of Iranian crude oil amount to nearly 45% of the Iranian government's budget, according to a U.S. government report from March 2025. Later this month, Beijing will send its Middle East envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia for visits "aimed at promoting peace talks (and) easing tensions," the foreign ministry said Wednesday. CBS/AFP Lebanese prime minister warns of "risks of renewed war," and of Lebanon being dragged in again In a message seemingly directed at the Iran-backed group Hezbollah, Lebanon's prime minister warned Wednesday against any moves that could pull the country into renewed fighting between Iran and the U.S. and Israel. "Faced with the risks of renewed war in the region, I renew my warning of the dangers of dragging Lebanon into a new senseless adventure in service of outside interests," Nawaf Salam said on Wednesday, without explicitly mentioning Hezbollah. Southern Lebanon has been a major front in the interlinked regional conflicts, with fighting between Iran's Hezbollah allies and Israel's military driving tens of thousands of people from their homes and killing almost 9,000 since Oct. 7, 2023, according to the Lebanese health ministry. Hezbollah, long a powerful political and paramilitary force in the country, pulled Lebanon directly into the war with Israel by launching strikes on the Jewish state in support of Hamas after the 2023 terror attacks sparked the war in Gaza, and then by firing rockets and missiles in support of Iran after joint U.S.-Israeli strikes commenced on Feb. 28. The Lebanon conflict has proven to be a major sticking point in negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, as Tehran has consistently rejected any peace deal with Washington that does not also end fighting in Lebanon and Gaza. A fragile ceasefire agreement reached between Israel and Hezbollah in June has halted most large-scale fighting between the two sides, but Israeli forces still occupy a large section of southern Lebanon, and there are sporadic attacks by both sides. "We do not accept the country again becoming a theater for the conflict of others," Salam added, saying Lebanon had "already paid a heavy price." President Trump threatened repeatedly ahead of the U.S. midterm elections to renew strikes on Iran, but he told the Financial Times as the results came in Tuesday evening that he had no immediate plans to order attacks. CBS/AFP Four tankers catch fire while transiting Strait of Hormuz, Iran's military says Four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's military said Wednesday, after it warned no one would benefit from a return to war. "Four non-compliant oil tankers attempting to pass through the prohibited passage south of the Strait of Hormuz were destroyed after striking naval mines and are still burning," Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement quoted by state TV. "Two other non-compliant ships or vessels have also been halted," they said The attacks come even as a diplomatic push is underway aimed at reaching a deal between the U.S. and Iran. Indirect talks via Qatari, Pakistani and Saudi mediators are understood to be underway. Although both sides previously expressed some hope of reaching an agreement, Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council on Tuesday cast doubt on progress toward a deal, calling the U.S. response to their demands "not convincing." CBS/AFP Iran says midterm results reflect rejection of war Iran's chief negotiator said Wednesday the midterm election results mean Americans have rejected the war with his country. "Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in a post on X. He cited the increased cost of living or "conscience" as two of the possible reasons for the widespread Republican losses in Tuesday's vote. "If the U.S. govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," Ghalibaf added. Trump acknowledges war with Iran partially to blame for GOP's election defeat President Trump acknowledged on Tuesday night that the war with Iran was partially responsible for the Republicans' defeat in the midterm elections. In a phone interview with Fox News, Mr. Trump said "part of it was Iran" when explaining the result of the elections, but that "at the same time, people understand the importance of what I've done." In a separate interview with the The Wall Street Journal , the president reiterated his comments and added that he does not regret starting the war with Tehran. "I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again," he told the newspaper. Qatar is said to expect feedback from U.S. and Iran on latest peace proposal within 36 hours Qatari mediators expect feedback within 36 hours from Iranian and U.S. negotiators on new ideas aimed at getting both sides closer to a deal to end the war, Reuters reported Tuesday, citing an official briefed on the talks. "The mediators came up with a new suggestion to move the process along, and it's currently being studied by the two sides," the official told Reuters. Efforts to reach a deal to prevent a return to fighting between Iran and the U.S. have ramped up recently. President Trump has said he is still open to an agreement, but has also threatened to resume major U.S. strikes after Tuesday's midterm elections in the U.S. On the eve of the elections, Mr. Trump again expressed hope that an agreement could still be reached, claiming Tehran wanted a settlement "as soon as possible." Iranian officials declared Monday that the ball "is in the U.S. court" and they said Iran's core demands to end the war would not be altered. item.title: World leaders question if GOP midterm losses will weaken or embolden Trump
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Capitals from Kyiv to Tehran were closely watching the U.S. midterm elections for clues about the direction of Washington’s foreign policy after two erratic years that have put many leaders in conflict with President Donald Trump. Those eager to see the president put on his back foot woke up Wednesday to find Republican losses even greater than they expected. But with Democrats set to control both houses of Congress, U.S. allies and foes alike are now wondering whether Trump - weakened and stymied at home - will act more aggressively or unpredictably on the world stage, where the executive has far more unilateral muscle, as he strives to secure a legacy in his remaining two years in office. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. A Democratic Congress could attempt to rein Trump in on several fronts, from imposing war powers restraints on Iran and further cutting back weapons sales and other aid to Israel, to constraining his tariff policies and resuming direct aid to Ukraine. Implications for war in the Middle East Tehran, which was hoping for a blow to Trump, now faces the question of whether the president - after such a resounding rebuke of his war policy at the ballot box - will still feel emboldened to resume strikes, as he has threatened in the run-up to the midterms. On Wednesday, Iranian officials portrayed the Republican defeat as a public verdict on an unpopular and costly war. “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the Iranian parliamentary speaker, said on X. Trump acknowledged Tuesday night that the war in Iran was partially to blame for wide-scale Republican losses in the midterm elections, but insisted the results were not a disavowal of his presidency. The midterm results sent ripples of concern through Israel, which had closely followed a U.S. election that was often dominated by bitter debates over the war, its effect on the U.S. economy, the role of pro-Israel campaign donors and allegations of antisemitism. Democratic candidates such as Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico, who won their Senate races in Michigan and Texas, respectively, have pledged to withhold weapons sales to Israel. They have also slammed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for a devastating Gaza campaign that has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians. The victories of so many Democrats who were critical of Netanyahu and Israel could spark “a sense of urgency” among Israeli opposition leaders to drop their differences and form a government to oust the current prime minister, said Yaakov Katz, a fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, a think tank in Jerusalem. Just last week, Israelis held their own elections and denied Netanyahu a straightforward return to power, but neither did they hand challenger Gadi Eisenkot an easy path to form a majority government. “This will have to have an impact on what’s happening with coalition building because you can’t ignore the huge shift in the U.S.,” Katz said. “It’s now in your face: The current government, if it continues, will only cause more problems and challenges for Israel. It’s just too toxic.” On Wednesday, several leaders from Eisenkot’s bloc pointed to the midterm results and blamed Netanyahu for cratering Israel’s image in the United States. The centrist Yair Lapid said that the midterm results showed the opposition bloc must not strike a deal to join a government that included Netanyahu - something that Netanyahu has been pushing. “The American election results in the morning have one unexpected outcome: they eliminate any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu,” Lapid said on X. “Israel cannot afford to let him remain prime minister. It endangers security, it endangers democracy, it will crush us in the world.” Yair Golan, a left-leaning opposition leader, said Netanyahu had become “toxic among both Democrats and Republicans.” Netanyahu remaining in power “could lead Israel down a path of international sanctions, international isolation, and a clash with the U.S., our friend and most important ally,” he warned. Europe considers a weakened Trump The war in Ukraine has been one of the widest partisan divides in U.S. foreign policy, and it will soon be put to the test as U.S.-brokered talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations resume in Abu Dhabi next week, the first such meeting since February. In Moscow, officials have treated the results as a sign that Trump’s position on Ukraine may harden in Moscow’s favor, arguing that by betting on a Democratic victory, Kyiv and European capitals have aligned themselves with Trump’s chief political enemies at home and should now expect two years of a less constrained president in return. “They will not get a more pliable and constrained Trump,” Konstantin Kosachev, a Russian senator, said on Telegram. “They will get a more determined one, who no longer has to look over his shoulder at elections. For all the importance of Congress, the US president’s role in foreign policy takes priority, and Trump knows that better than everyone else put together.” The questions about Washington’s commitments to NATO and its other traditional allies, which emerged during Trump’s first presidency, led some Europeans back then to warn that U.S. interests inevitably would diverge from their own. Those differences have come into starker relief during Trump’s second term, as he pressed Europe to take responsibility for more of its own defense, turning his sights to Asia and the Middle East and away from Russia’s war in Ukraine. Now, European officials are urging their governments to stay the course as they seek to continue reducing their reliance on the U.S. as the continent’s key security guarantor. “Weakened Trump could become more aggressive and unpredictable. A lame duck could quickly turn into an angry duck,” Bernd Lange, a member of the European Parliament, said on X. “For EU, this is an opportunity and warning. More democratic influence could bring greater predictability and dialogue. But US protectionism won’t disappear. EU cannot live at Trump’s mercy!” The British government was careful to avoid showing any official pleasure with the Democratic takeover of Congress, knowing Trump is not yet halfway through his term. Privately, some officials expressed relief that that U.S. voters had delivered a check on a mercurial president who has upended transatlantic trade and security and produced a spike in fuel costs following his Iran war. And they expressed fear over how Trump - who seemed unleashed at the beginning of his second term - might act if he feels hemmed in by a hostile Congress. “You have to be aware that any president will still have enormous power to execute his foreign policy even if he finds himself more constrained by Democratic Congress at home,” said a British official who spoke on the condition of anonymity in order to share candid views. “Certainly, with this president, you have to be prepared for him to be even more volatile after this.” The view that Europe cannot afford to depend on Washington’s goodwill was echoed across Western Europe, where many called for continued support for Ukraine as a means of ensuring security on the continent. “Not because everything now changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and relations with the rest of the world,” European Parliament vice president Christel Schaldemose said on X. “But the EU must ⁠continue the course of standing stronger and standing on its own two feet. That’s not up for debate.” The issue has gained urgency as Trump’s own backing for Kyiv has faltered, at times leading him to lash out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, whom he has blamed for the global energy disruptions even though the war in Iran has been the main contributor. Measured reactions in Asia The midterms are not expected to fundamentally change Washington’s approach to China, given the bipartisan consensus on strategic competition with Beijing, and across the region the prevailing expectation is that U.S. protectionist policies will continue regardless of who controls Congress. In Beijing, officials stuck to China’s traditional neutrality, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning calling the elections a domestic U.S. affair. She said Beijing was willing to work with Washington to “strengthen communication and manage differences.” Some analysts suggested that while the election would do little to the overall approach to China, it could still change how that competition plays out. “A Democratic-led Congress will certainly further intensify pressure on China on Taiwan, AI and export controls,” Zhao Minghao, a professor at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, told the South China Morning Post, adding that Democrats would likely scrutinize Trump’s engagement with Beijing more closely and could use China policy to challenge him politically. “This is a very big challenge for Beijing,” Zhao said, warning that Trump’s diminishing political authority could undermine recent progress toward a more stable relationship. Steve Hendrix, Natalia Abbakumova, Suzan Haidamous, Mohamad El Chamaa, Rudy Lu and Greg Miller contributed to this report. item.title: Mike Johnson won't seek reelection as House Republican leader
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats are riding their sweep of Congress into a new era, eager to meet voter demands for change with plans to tackle high costs of living and confront President Donald Trump's final years in the White House. In a nationwide romp, Democrats ousted Republicans from coast to coast , with many surprising places in between, as voters rejected the president's party for the promise of something different for the country. Their majorities will be padded by wide margins in both the House and the Senate. The results set up a divided government, with Congress poised to reassert itself as a coequal branch ready to challenge Trump and reverse course after two years of unified GOP control. "We hear you," said House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who would make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job when the new Congress begins on Jan. 3, 2027. "We're going to work hard to deliver on the dramatic change that you deserve," he said. The tally was decisive, at times bewildering, for the staggering scope of Democratic gains and the depth of Republican losses. The swelling margins underlined a deep sense of voter anger and concern over the economy and the state of democracy . All told, the results present a fundamental reshaping of power in Washington, with new opportunities and challenges for governing. Vice President JD Vance blamed war in Iran for Republican midterm losses. Trump struck a conciliatory tone, suggesting he could work with the Democrats, but he also warned of gridlock ahead as he threatened to use the power of the presidential veto to strike down their agenda. "I don't want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything," he told Politico. House Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek reelection as House Republican leader following the Democrats' win, according to two people familiar with his plans who insisted on anonymity to disclose them. Democrats vow a 100-day agenda and investigations of Trump House Democrats are promising a 100-day agenda starting with efforts to lower the costs of gas, groceries and other goods, as well as bills to reverse cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid healthcare programs. They're also ready to launch a robust oversight agenda to, as Jeffries says, "hold the crooks accountable." Impeachment — of the president or his Cabinet members — is an option. The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, issued a one-sentence warning: "Lawyer up." Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, issued his own one-word missive: "Subpoenas." Democrats will be under pressure to quickly show that they have solutions for the high gas and grocery prices , the war in Iran and concerns about the direction of the country. For Jeffries and his leadership team, it will be their first time in the majority, managing a class of newcomers including a handful of far-left democratic socialists . With the majority in the 435-member House well past the 218 needed and the Senate Democrats holding at least 54 of 100 seats in that chamber, Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer will have room to maneuver. "Five words for the American people: Relief is on the way," the New York senator said. A lame-duck session and leadership elections await Republicans For Republicans, their shriveled numbers will create a reckoning of their own, as they try to figure out what went so uniformly wrong. Johnson had quipped he may return to his Louisiana hometown of Shreveport to start a lawn care company if the Republicans lost power. Rivals seek to replace him. Republicans may be anxious during the post-election lame-duck sprint to accomplish as much as possible in their remaining weeks in power. But hopes for another GOP-only priority package like their big tax breaks and spending cuts bill seem dim as defeated lawmakers prepare to go home at the end of the year. Conservatives have also eyed the opportunity for Trump to nominate another justice to the Supreme Court while Senate Republicans still hold a majority. However, no current justice has announced any intent to step aside. And the government could be headed toward a federal shutdown next month if Congress fails to pass a funding bill to keep operations running. In the weeks ahead, the parties will hold internal leadership elections as members-elect arrive for freshman orientation at the Capitol. The House will choose its speaker as one of the first votes when the new Congress convenes. Vance cites the Iran war for Republicans' losses In a lengthy online post, the vice president seemingly sought to distance himself from election results seen as a referendum on Trump that featured big Republican losses across the country. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote, adding, "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest." Trailblazers are coming to Congress Rarely has the president's party held on to power during midterm elections, but the Democratic sweep carried echoes of Trump's first term, when Republicans faced a voter revolt that sent Democrats to the House majority , and the Barack Obama era, when the Republican tea party swept to power. This new Congress will also mark firsts and welcome trailblazers . With the election of Democrat Julia Stratton of Illinois, the Senate will for the first time have three Black women in office. Democrat Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota will be the first Native American female senator, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire will become the first openly gay male U.S. senator and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan will be the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate . ___ Associated Press writers Tom Beaumont, Joey Cappelletti, Jill Colvin, Kevin Freking, Mary Clare Jalonick and Will Weissert contributed to this report. ___ Follow the AP's coverage of the 2026 elections at https://apnews.com/hub/elections . LONDON (AP) — Mysterious cyberattacks on European supermarket fridges have sent officials around the continent scrambling to figure out the cold, hard facts. Supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros). One Swedish supermarket said its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit). It's a repeat of an earlier incident that struck refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands. Here's a closer look: What happened and who was affected Supermarkets in at least half a dozen European countries, including Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, Italy and Estonia, reported problems on Monday. It wasn't just big chains. The owner of a butcher shop in Athens told private Greek Skai TV Tuesday that someone hacked into the temperature control of a refrigeration unit, raising the temperature to 150 degrees Celsius (302 degrees Fahrenheit). George Boubas said his employees who start their shift at 4 a.m. at the shop in the Kifisia suburb first noticed the problem. It took a technician two hours to wrest back control of the unit’s temperature settings, although the meat products weren’t affected, he said. Boubas said the technician told him that an area supermarket and a fast-food restaurant experienced the same issue. He said they resorted to switching off the Wi-Fi connection to the refrigeration units to restrict outside access. Experts said the cyberattacks were a reminder of the risks that come as more things get connected to the internet. “This attack is a wake-up call. We have filled our homes and shops with devices that are really small computers, yet we still treat them like ordinary appliances," said Katerina Mitrokotsa, a cybersecurity professor at the University of St. Gallen, in Switzerland. “A fridge doesn’t look like a security risk, and that’s exactly why attackers like it.” Fridges are connected to save money and cut waste The cyberattack mirrors one that happened weeks earlier that affected mainly French and Dutch retailers. French cybersecurity investigators blamed problems with outdated remote control modules made by Danish company Danfoss as well as U.S.-based Copeland. Danfoss said most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates, while Copeland identified a vulnerability in discontinued controllers. “Supermarkets connect their fridges so they can monitor temperatures around the clock across hundreds of stores, get alerts before food spoils, cut energy costs and let technicians fix faults remotely," Mitrokotsa said. "This saves money and reduces food waste, but every connected fridge is also an entry point that needs to be secured like any other IT system.” Experts said many businesses are rushing to embrace trendy new technology while neglecting the vast network of connections that they rely on for their daily operations, from payment and ordering systems to warehouses, refrigeration and other building controls. “Organizations are pouring budget into AI and digital transformation while the systems that keep food cold, water clean, and lights on often run on hardware that has not been funded since installation," said Nicole Carignan, senior vice president of security and AI strategy at cybersecurity company Darktrace. “Nobody broke into these refrigeration systems with a zero-day," she said, using a term for a flaw that has gone undetected by the system’s creators and security reviews. "They got in through internet-facing controllers, end-of-life firmware, and default passwords. That is technical debt coming due.” British cybersecurity officials on Tuesday shed little light on the latest attack, while pointing to what they called “legacy technology.” “The cyberattack on French supermarkets was a result of exploitation of known vulnerabilities,” U.K. cyber minister Liz Lloyd said in a speech. “It’s a clear demonstration that poor cyber hygiene, like weak passwords, continues to put organizations at risk.” Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Center, told reporters the French fridges were "connected directly to the internet with default passwords.” A team from the center issued warnings and worked through Monday night contacting organizations that had “vulnerable technology exposed,” he said. No evidence so far that AI was involved Advanced artificial intelligence systems from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have come under fire recently after a string of revelations that they hacked into organizations while evading human control. Experts, however, said Tuesday that they didn't think these attacks were powered by AI. “There is no evidence AI was used, and the techniques did not require it,” said Carignan. “I think the key element of that is that this wasn’t an AI attack” said Paul Chichester, director of operations at the U.K. cyber center. “This is using vulnerabilities that absolutely have been out there for a long period of time. And that’s where we really need to sort of focus on.” Who’s behind it and what's the motive Investigations have so far failed to discover who might have carried out the cyberattacks and why. France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, said it has been investigating refrigeration-system breaches since mid-October and coordinating protective measures with “all sectors that could be affected.” In a statement to The Associated Press, the agency said it knew of compromised remote refrigeration controllers in Danfoss’s AK-SM and AK-SC ranges, as well as Copeland and Dixell xweb systems. ANSSI said it was mobilized to assist “potential victims in France” and pointed to a security alert first published Oct. 12, which has been updated regularly. Italian cybersecurity and intelligence officials were scheduled to meet Tuesday morning to discuss the incident, according to Italian news agency ANSA. Officials at the European Union's executive Commission were also holding similar meetings. European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier declined on Tuesday to comment on who might have carried out the hacks, saying that's up to the bloc's 27 national authorities to figure out. Regnier told reporters the incidents “are not isolated” and that Europeans "have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents.” ___ Hadjicostis reported from Nicosia, Cyprus. AP writers Lorne Cook in Brussels, Lefteris Pitarakis in Athens and Thomas Adamson in Paris contributed to this report. item.title: Hegseth faces impeachment vote as Democrats prepare to take power
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON – Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth faces impeachment accusations when Congress returns after the midterm elections and others, including President Donald Trump , could be investigated for alleged misconduct as Democrats return to power. Besides Trump and Hegseth, lawmakers have already filed impeachment resolutions against Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Education Secretary Linda McMahon . None of the resolutions gained traction while Republicans led the House, but they signal what Democrats could investigate when they take control of the House and Senate in January. The House impeached Trump twice while led by Democrats during his first term, over his dealings with Ukraine and over the Capitol attack on Jan. 6, 2021 . The Senate acquitted him both times for lack of a 2/3 majority to convict. But Democrats have filed at least four more impeachment resolutions against him for potential investigation. Impeachments have become more common but convictions remain elusive Any House member can introduce a resolution proposing to impeach the president, vice president, other executive officials or judges with accusations of "treason, bribery or other high crimes and misdemeanors." The process has led to the removal of eight federal judges but not anyone from the executive branch. Three presidents − including Bill Clinton in 1998 and Andrew Johnson in 1868 − and War Secretary William Belknap in 1876 have been impeached but not convicted. House Speaker Mike Johnson , R-Louisiana, has predicted another impeachment push against Trump with Democrats holding the gavel. Trump has said he expects to be impeached again with Democrats in control of House . He invited another showdown in June 2025 with the taunt: "go ahead and try Impeaching me, again, MAKE MY DAY!" Hegseth accused of unauthorized war in Iran, Venezuela Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky, launched his eight impeachment accusations against Hegseth on Sept. 15. The difference from other resolutions filed against Trump and his Cabinet secretaries months ago is that Massie plans to force a House vote on the measure as early as next week, when lawmakers return from the midterm elections. The Republican majority could kill it by voting to table it. But Massie accused Hegseth of conducting the war against Iran without congressional authorization, seizing Venezuela’s President Nicolas Maduro without constitutional authority and killing suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean without judicial authorization. "Secretary Hegseth's constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran,” said Massie, who lost his Republican primary and has only the lame duck session of Congress to pursue the impeachment resolution. “He is abusing the power of his office to ignore congressional war powers resolutions, to kidnap foreign leaders and to intimidate critics of the Trump administration by retaliating against them for exercising free speech.” Trump has defended Hegseth. "I think it's terrible. All they do is they talk about impeaching everybody," Trump told reporters Oct. 28 . "He's doing a great job. He's a great warrior. I think he's the best at his job in many many years and a lot of people agree with that." More: Trump's stinging midterm rebuke casts a new political landscape Congress could potentially move quickly if there is support for Massie's resolution. The House impeached Trump a week after the Capitol riot Jan. 6, 2021, and a week before he left office. The Senate acquitted him at trial in mid-February 2021. Trump would have been barred from federal office if convicted. Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in response to Massie's resolution that Hegseth is a "transformative leader" who has returned standards to the military and made the country's arsenal stronger than ever. "The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first," she said in a statement to USA TODAY . Wilson had called an earlier Democratic impeachment resolution "another charade in an attempt to distract the American people from the major successes we have had here at the Department of War." Trump, who endorsed Massie’s Republican primary opponent, has called him a “loser,” a "lightweight" and "a major sleazebag" for opposing the Iran war and voting against other administration priorities. Raskin outlines potential investigations of Trump Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, who led the second impeachment against Trump, argued that Trump has "undoubtedly" committed impeachable offenses. He cited the unauthorized war against Iran, spending money Congress hasn't authorized and bulldozing the East Wing of the White House. "They have been plundering money from our government in the most massively corrupt presidential administration in American history," Raskin told NBC's "Meet the Press." Raskin called impeachment "a critical tool in the toolbox" but that Congress could respond to Trump legislatively, too. "Impeachment is not a taboo with us, it's not a fetish with us, we understand it is not a panacea," Raskin said. "We will not hesitate to use it if we need to use it." Departing Democrats accuse Trump of unauthorized war, abuse of power and profiting from office Democrats have filed at least four impeachment resolutions against Trump during his second term. All four lawmakers have lost their seats, so the resolutions signal subjects for investigation next year. Rep. Shri Thanedar of Michigan, who lost his Democratic primary after four years in office, filed impeachment accusations against Trump in April 2025 . His accusations included alleged obstruction of justice from Trump firing Justice Department staffers who investigated Jan. 6 and for dropping charges against New York Mayor Eric Adams. Rep. John Larson of Connecticut, who lost his Democratic primary after 28 years in office, filed impeachment accusations against Trump in April for alleged belligerence without congressional authorization against Iran, Yemen, Lebanon, Syria, Nigeria and Gaza, and for threatening military force against Panama, Colombia, Cuba and Greenland. Larson also accused Trump of abuse of power in the immigration crackdown and of twisting law enforcement to investigate perceived political rivals. Rep. Al Green of Texas, who lost his Democratic primary after 22 years in office after Republicans redrew congressional maps in his state, has filed several impeachment resolutions against Trump , the latest in August over the seizure of Maduro . Rep. Steve Cohen, D-Tennessee, filed 26 impeachment accusations against Trump on Sept. 24 . Beyond the military allegations, Cohen accused Trump of abuse of power for his immigration crackdown, for his investigation of perceived rivals such as former FBI Director James Comey and for profiting from his office. “Trump is clearly the most impeachable President our country has ever endured," said Cohen, another longtime Trump antagonist who retired from his 20-year seat after GOP redistricting. "His continued presence in office is a danger to our democracy." Education Secretary McMahon accused of dismantling department but she aims to improve student performance Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, D-Oregon, filed impeachment allegations against Education Secretary Linda McMahon in June. The accusations covered significant staff reductions at the department and moving 140 programs and offices to other federal departments. “I introduced an impeachment resolution because Secretary McMahon has made it her mission to close down the Department of Education, something she does not have the right to do,” Bonamici said on the House floor. Trump has said he appointed McMahon to dismantle the department . McMahon responded to the impeachment allegations by arguing that Democrats were fine with historically low test scores, classrooms shuttered during the COVID-19 pandemic and allowing transgender athletes in female locker rooms. “It speaks volumes that House Democrats think an impeachable offense is working to improve student outcomes and reduce the federal bureaucracy,” McMahon said on social media in June . “To the Democrats in Congress: do better.” Health Secretary Kennedy accused of 'spreading conspiracy theories' but spokesperson calls allegations 'partisan theatrics' Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Michigan, filed impeachment accusations against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in December. Stevens accused Kennedy of freezing or canceling billions of dollars in research, firing health advisers and spreading conspiracy theories. " Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has imperiled the health and safety of the American people, eroded public confidence in the nation’s public health institutions and stalled decades of scientific and medical progress ," Stevens wrote in the resolution. Andrew Nixon, the top department spokesperson, accused Stevens, who lost a Democratic primary for Senate this year and later endorsed the Republican opponent in the race , of playing political games. "Secretary Kennedy remains focused on improving Americans’ health and lowering costs, not on partisan theatrics designed to elevate standing in a failing, third-rate Senate bid," Nixon said in a statement to USA TODAY . item.title: GOP officials describe 'reckoning' to come after party's midterm losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump's allies on Wednesday tiptoed their way toward once unthinkable territory: blaming the president. The unusual candor followed sweeping GOP defeats across the country, a repudiation of the president that matched some of the party's worst fears. Some pointed to the Iran war and its effect on gas and grocery prices. Others pointed to the president's demeanor. "There's a little bit of a reckoning in the Republican Party about where they go," said Matt Dole, chair of the GOP in deep red Licking County, Ohio. "I think you're going to see a part of the Republican Party advocate for a return to normalcy, which is not repudiating Trump's ideology and policies, but will repudiate Trump's style." "It sounds a little ironic," failed Maine Republican Gov. candidate Bobby Charles told POLITICO. "but I am nevertheless optimistic for the future because Trump's going to be gone in two years." The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump and his advisors, meanwhile, blamed a myriad of factors, including Fox News, RINOs and "lazy" candidates — even as the party resoundingly lost both chambers of government and the blue wave rolled through deep red Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Kansas. Trump singled out Texas GOP governor Greg Abbott, who he called a "RINO," and absolved himself of blame, claiming Republicans would have won "in a landslide" had he been on the ballot. Abbott did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump's adviser Alex Bruesewitz blamed the GOP's poor performance on candidates he described as "uninspiring, lazy and thoroughly ineffective communicators" — explicitly calling out Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who struggled throughout the course of his campaign to gain traction against Democratic incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff. The Collins campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. One GOP operative working on multiple midterm races said it was a "lazy excuse" to blame candidate quality. "This is more than just one lazy candidate here. I mean, the chair of the … NRCC is losing his election." Still, other Republicans turned their ire on the GOP-controlled Congress. "The Republican Party needs to have a conversation with itself about how to listen to the voters and present meaningful policy reform that impacts their lives," said Gina Swoboda, the former chair of Arizona's Republican Party and a longtime Trump ally. "This Congress did not do a single thing that I can name that meaningfully impacted the working class and middle class." Bruesewitz expressed dismay that some of those candidates boarded Air Force One and left their states five days before Election Day, after Trump had traveled to campaign for them. "They're so dependent and so reliant on the president," Bruesewitz said. "The president's strength has allowed Republicans to coast for a decade. His endorsement has cleared the field for them in their primaries and oftentimes in general elections. Most of them have never had to fight in a tough race, so they forgot the basics of campaigning and communicating in a digital era." Top Trump officials had already hinted at that plan in interviews with POLITICO in the lead up to the election. Republicans on Capitol Hill and beyond, who have been preparing for the bloodbath and recriminations, were not buying it. They argued that flat characterization of Republican candidates as lazy could not possibly be applied to every vulnerable Republican who lost — and that Trump and the aides around him ought to look in the mirror. But tellingly, they refused to put their name behind it. "We are beyond candidate quality. It's a bloodbath," one senior Senate GOP official said. "Trump did this." A Republican operative working on swing state campaigns said Tuesday was a perfect storm "of just incompetence." "The people in the White House didn't do anything to stop him from engaging on things that were actively making everything worse because he was ignoring what the voters were caring about," the operative said. item.title: Trump faces a political reckoning after Democrats' midterm rout
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump spent two months urging Americans to pretend he was on the ballot. On Tuesday, they did just that. Voters delivered a stunning rebuke to Trump's party that rivaled anything Republicans had suffered in 50 years, defeats on ruby-red turf that Trump won handily just two years ago, where he has dominated politics for nearly a decade and against candidates he had in some cases handpicked. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Not only did Democrats flip Senate and governor seats in red states, but at times by eye-popping margins. "The message is very clear and very simple here. It was a complete repudiation of the party as defined by Donald Trump," said Mike Murphy, a Los Angeles-based Republican consultant who worked for candidates in the pre-Trump GOP, including Jeb Bush and John McCain. "We have a little saying in show business, 'box office poison,' and that's what Donald Trump has become." More than 41 times in recent weeks, The Washington Post found, Trump told voters to act this November as if the midterms were a referendum on him - a bold dare for a president whose approval ratings had reached historic lows as a growing number of Americans reported opposing his policies and his behavior in office. In just two years since Trump's remarkable presidential victory campaign, in which he vowed to lower consumer prices, he has generated deep resentment of his policies. Voters blamed his decision to go to war against Iran and his tariff policies for raising prices, instead. Trump left himself no hedge against being held responsible for voter unhappiness because he had molded the GOP into his image over the last decade. He demanded complete loyalty from Republicans and sought to cast out those who opposed him. Then he made himself the face of the party's midterm messaging, not only calling for his advisers to feature him in midterm television advertisements but demanding that the GOP host a first-of-its-kind midterm convention to tout his policies. Trump "brought a Chernobyl-level disaster to the Republican Party," Murphy said, "the worst beating the party has taken since '74, after Watergate." That year, Democrats gained 49 seats in the House and four in the Senate, on the heels of newly installed President Gerald Ford's pardon of Richard M. Nixon and amid a spike in gas prices and overall inflation. So far this year, with some races left to be called, Democrats have flipped seven Senate seats and at least 25 in a House with far fewer competitive seats. They also flipped several governorships and state legislative chambers. In Texas on Tuesday, James Talarico's double-digit lead over Trump's chosen Senate candidate Ken Paxton was particularly symbolic, taking place in a state long seen as the heartland of the conservative movement. In North Carolina, a state Trump won three times, Democrat Roy Cooper not only flipped a Senate seat but was leading early Wednesday by nearly 20 percentage points. Democrats snatched Senate seats in other deeply red states, including South Carolina and Kansas. In Pennsylvania, the swing state that sealed Trump's comeback victory, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro was winning reelection by 22 points with nearly all the vote counted. For months, Trump's advisers insisted that he was the key to Republicans' being able to defy poor expectations in the midterms. Trump, they argued, could rally Republicans to the polls like no other and was responsible for assembling a coalition that included young and diverse voters that the GOP had never dreamed of winning. Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters dubbed the September GOP midterm convention in Dallas as "Trumpapalooza." "Everything that the president has done regarding the economy, regarding the average American worker, I think will lead to votes in November," Gruters told Newsmax later that month. The votes went toward Democrats. "Midterm elections are about anger management and failed expectations. They drive the math of turnout," said Paul Shumaker, a Republican strategist in North Carolina, where Democrats flipped the seat held by retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis. "Clearly, Trump failed to meet the economic expectations and also fueled the anger in doing so," he said. By mid-October, Trump's standing with voters had fallen to levels not seen since Harry S. Truman. In a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, the share of U.S. adults who approved of his overall job performance fell to 33 percent, with 66 percent disapproving; 52 percent said they disapproved strongly. Only 28 percent said they approved of his handling of the economy and 27 percent approved of his handling of "the situation with Iran." An even smaller share, 28 percent, said they approved of Trump's MAGA movement. By more than 2 to 1, Americans said they felt Trump had "gone beyond his authority" as president. The poll found that registered voters, 58 percent to 39 percent, said they would rather have a Democratic-led Congress acting as a check on Trump than a Republican one to support his agenda. That margin was roughly double what it had been a year earlier. Unlike notable midterm defeats in 1994 and 2006, when President Bill Clinton and George W. Bush publicly accepted blame for their parties' defeats and committed to changing course in governing, Trump did no such thing. "I don't like to consider it a defeat for me. I wasn't on the ballot," Trump told Fox News late Tuesday night, a message that was the opposite of what he spent weeks saying on the campaign trail. "There was a mood in the air, I guess," he continued. "I shouldn't feel guilty because … no matter how good the president is, you lose" in the midterms. Like Trump, White House advisers blamed the losses entirely on the Republican candidates, insisting that rather than being a rebuke of Trump, the outcome was merely a function of his not being on the ballot. The White House distributed a statement Tuesday night arguing Trump "did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates themselves." "Bloodbath doesn't even begin to describe" voters' reaction to Republicans, said Barrett Marson, an Arizona-based GOP strategist. It was "a complete and total repudiation of one man and his policies," he said, by "an electorate that is upset with being told by President Trump that they are doing better than they are." "It didn't work for Joe Biden, and Tuesday showed it was the absolute worst strategy Donald Trump could deploy." The president had failed to explain some of his policies to the public, said Rep. Ralph Norman (R-South Carolina), who lost a primary to Sen. Darline Graham, the Trump-endorsed candidate who lost on Tuesday. "The Iran war - he needs to explain," Norman said. "When I heard him say, 'The war will end when I say it's going to end,' I'm sorry, that's prideful." Elon Musk contributed nearly half a billion dollars to Republican political efforts this cycle (Kent NISHIMURA) Tech billionaire Elon Musk joked on Wednesday about Republicans' defeat in US midterm elections after spending hundreds of millions of dollars to help the party. Democrats seized control of the US Congress on Tuesday, capturing both the Senate and House of Representatives in a stunning rejection of President Donald Trump's political agenda. "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," Musk said on X, including the shrug emoji. Musk contributed nearly half a billion dollars to Republican political efforts, making him the largest individual contributor in a federal election cycle since unlimited election spending was allowed in 2010, according to campaign finance tracker OpenSecrets. His donations have mostly gone to his Republican-leaning America PAC, as well as to the Republican Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) super PAC. The SLF used Musk's $158 million in donations in September to support Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas. The Texas Senate election topped the list in terms of expenditure, with Paxton's Democrat challenger James Talarico facing more than $200 million in opposition from outside spending groups. Talarico defeated Paxton, a close ally of Trump, to become the first Democrat to win statewide office in Texas since 1994. He took aim at Musk at a victory rally in Austin. "In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths. The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world and the entire Washington, DC establishment," Talarico said. He also targeted billionaires "who own the social media algorithms, who own the cable news networks, who own the politicians fighting on our screens" and who "want us at each other's throats." - 'Billionaire's world' - Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated incumbent Texas Governor Greg Abbott in another blow to the deeply conservative southern border state. Hinojosa said she asked at the start of her campaign if Texas was "a state that is by and for the people of Texas." "Or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Does Texas belong to the parents and their children? Or the billionaires trying to dismantle our schools? Does Texas belong to the farmers and ranchers who have worked this land for generations? Or the corporations trying to buy it up?" she said after her victory. Talarico and Hinojosa both campaigned on tighter regulations for AI data centers. The spread of data centers across Texas has become a central issue as residents worry about rising electricity bills, water use and strain on the power grid. Musk has moved the headquarters of his comapanies Tesla, SpaceX and X to Texas. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk joked on X after the result. The Supreme Court ruled in 2010 that the government cannot limit political spending by corporations, unions and other groups if they spend it independently of candidates. A lower court decision ruled that these organizations could also raise an unlimited amount of money from donors. Now, big donors can allocate vast sums of money to try to influence elections and remain anonymous by donating through secondary organizations. item.title: Democrats seize control of Congress. The shift goes far beyond swing states.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
It was a blue wave big enough to become a blue tsunami. On Tuesday, the Democratic Party shattered a series of decades-long Republican winning streaks, notched several historic firsts and flipped both the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives as Americans in states and districts that voted to reelect President Trump just two years ago delivered a harsh judgment on the steep tariffs, rising gas prices, aggressive immigration raids and unresolved war in Iran that have so far dominated his second term. "We didn't win this race by alienating our neighbors or shaming our neighbors or ridiculing our neighbors," Democrat James Talarico said after winning the Senate election in Texas. "We embodied a new kind of politics. A politics rooted in a deep love for our state, for our country and, most importantly, for all of our neighbors." U.S. Sen.-elect James Talarico speaks during a midterm election night event at the Long Center for the Performing Arts on Nov. 3, 2026, in Austin, Texas. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Votes were still being tallied and key races remained uncalled as Election Day came to an end. But as of 1 a.m. ET on Wednesday, when the last polls closed in Alaska, Democrats were projected to gain more than three dozen seats in the House and as many as nine seats in the Senate — far beyond the three and four seats, respectively, that they needed to retake each chamber. They were also on track to win the majority of governorships for the first time since 2011. The list of milestones was long: The first Texas Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate since 1988 (Talarico). The first Latina ever elected governor of the Lone Star State (Gina Hinojosa). Kansas's first Democratic senator since the Great Depression (Adam Hamilton). The first Black woman governor in U.S. history (Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms). The first Democratic senator from South Carolina in decades (Annie Andrews). America's first Muslim senator (Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan). And what could be the largest Democratic House majority since 2008. As a result, Trump will no longer enjoy complete Republican control of Congress. Starting in January, Democrats in the House and Senate will have the power to block parts of the president's agenda, reject his nominees, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again) . Historically, midterms tend to be backlash elections; a president's party almost always sheds House seats when voters return to the polls to rate his first two years in office. The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six . Yet some midterms are more momentous than others. In 2006, President George W. Bush's second midterm, Republicans lost 31 seats. In 2010, President Barack Obama's first midterm, Democrats lost 64 seats. And in 2018, Trump's first midterm, Republicans lost 42 seats. Attendees cheer and wave flags during an election night event with Sen. Jon Ossoff in Atlanta on Nov. 3, 2026. Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images This year, according to data journalist G. Elliott Morris , "Democrats have won the largest House popular vote victory for any party since 1974, when the Watergate scandal rocked Republicans to their core." Here are four takeaways that help explain what happened in the 2026 midterms, and why. Red state revolt The most striking thing about this year's Democratic gains is that they came in some of the redder parts of the country. Before Election Day, the GOP's majorities on Capitol Hill were already narrow — a dynamic that usually limits the opposing party's pickup opportunities. A Republican-friendly 2026 Senate map and an unprecedented mid-decade GOP redistricting push further reduced the number of easy targets for Democrats. Yet high prices, an unpopular war and Trump's falling approval ratings gave Democrats a chance to compete in places where they haven't prevailed in years — or, in some cases, decades. Strong nominees went on to capitalize Tuesday night. In Texas, Talarico, a 37-year-old state lawmaker and former seminarian, defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, a MAGA favorite with a controversial past. In Kansas, Hamilton, a 61-year-old megachurch pastor and former Republican, defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall. In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek, a state lawmaker and two-time Paralympic gold medalist who describes himself as a "prairie populist," defeated GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former local news anchor. In South Carolina, Andrews, a pediatrician, defeated incumbent Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after the recent death of her brother, longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted to book a return ticket to the U.S. Senate, where he previously served from 2007 to 2025. South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews speaks during her election night watch party in Charleston, S.C., on Nov. 3, 2026. Mic Smith/AP Democrat Scott Colom was even leading incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi by a handful of votes. These are not the types of races Democrats typically win. Trump won Ohio by 11 points in 2024. He won Iowa by 13 points. He won Texas by 14. He won Kansas by 16. He won South Carolina by 18. He won Mississippi by 24. He won North Carolina — where former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper breezed to victory — by 3. Whether the 2026 results foreshadow some sort of larger rural realignment — or just a temporary rebuke of Trump's current policies — remains to be seen. But either way, Tuesday's blue tsunami swept well into red America. The Trump effect Before Election Day, the president urged his supporters to vote like he was on the ballot. Afterward, he wrote on social media , "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" But preliminary exit polls suggested that even if Americans couldn't technically cast their votes for — or against — Trump this time around, his performance and policies were very much top of mind. A full 62% of midterm voters said they disapproved of how Trump is handling his job as president. Just 38% said they approved. No recent president has emerged from a midterm election with an approval rating that low . Nearly 90% of voters said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote; about the same number said they were concerned about the price of gas and groceries. Nearly two-thirds said that Trump's policies, including tariffs, have made the U.S. economy worse and that going to war with Iran was the wrong decision. More than half said Trump is not a strong leader, does not fight for people like them, does not have the right priorities and does not have the mental capability to serve effectively as president. Meanwhile, Trump did little to boost Republican chances on Election Day. His endorsements and interventions appeared to backfire in contest after contest . He attracted more attention in the closing days of the campaign for praising certain candidates' anatomy than for promoting his party's agenda. And he spent his final appearance before Nov. 3 talking about his troubled reflecting pool project . Trump has defied history before. But in the end, 2026 seemed to show that even his powers have their limits. In 2006, President George W. Bush's Republicans lost both the House and the Senate after Americans soured on another Middle Eastern war. Something similar happened again on Tuesday. Swing voters swung — hard The big story of the 2024 presidential election was how a rightward shift among previously left-leaning independents and Latinos helped propel Trump back to the presidency. It appears both groups have shifted back. According to Equis, a polling firm that focuses on Latino voters, Democrats increased their overall share of the Latino vote by 10 points in 2026 (65%) compared to 2024 (55%). In some states, like Virginia (+19 points) and New Jersey (+23 points), Democratic gains among Latinos were even bigger. In others, like Texas (60%) and Florida (56%), Democrats went from losing the Latino vote last time to winning it. Those gains likely contributed to key House victories in both states and major statewide wins in Texas. As for self-identified independents, Trump split them about evenly with Democrat Kamala Harris two years ago . This time around, independents appear to have favored Democrats by roughly 17 percentage points . Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff waves to supporters during an election night rally after winning reelection. Carlos Barria/Reuters A new generation of Democrats For decades, Democrats have lamented their party's gerontocracy, from the Silent Generation stalwarts who long led their congressional caucus to the baby boomer candidates who seem to keep winning their presidential nominations. But Tuesday's tsunami has provided the party with a whole new batch of " elder Millennial " stars, including Talarico (37), El-Sayed (42), Andrews (45), Turek (47), Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (44) and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (39), whose cruise to reelection has inspired buzz about a possible presidential bid (which he has publicly ruled out). Before Nov. 3, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani were among the most prominent Democrats representing the party's next generation on the national stage. Now they have company.
